summary: Integrated telecoms are slow-growing, cash-generating carriers that are spending heavily to move customers onto fiber. Q3 2026 reports were solid: Verizon's adjusted EBITDA rose 8.0% on revenue growth of 1.5% [1], AT&T added a record 769,000 internet customers, 442,000 of them on fiber [2], and Deutsche Telekom raised guidance [3]. FactSet puts Diversified Telecommunication Services revenue growth below 1% for the quarter [4]. Leverage is the constraint, at 3.13x net debt to EBITDA for AT&T [2]. Lumen is the weak spot, with revenue down 12% [5]. We found no sourced forward P/E for this sub-industry.

watch: AT&T's net debt to EBITDA was 3.13x in Q3 against a target of returning to the 2.5x range during 2029, so buybacks and a $23-24bn 2026 capital plan have to be funded within that limit [2].
Lumen's Q3 free cash flow excluding special items was minus $76M, and its 2026 free cash flow guide of $1.9-2.1B includes $729M of divestiture proceeds [5].
Telefonica lowered its 2026 revenue growth target to 1-1.5% from 1.5-2.5% while raising profit targets, and its German revenue and EBITDA are still falling [6].
BT's first-half normalised free cash flow fell 59% to about 0.2bn pounds while Openreach lost 366,000 broadband lines in the half [7].
Fixed wireless held 9.1% of US fixed connections at end-2025, and Verizon, AT&T and cable all sell it, so it is both a growth product and a threat to fiber pricing [9][1].

basics.intro: Integrated telecoms run the networks that carry voice and data to homes, businesses and other carriers. They earn money from monthly subscriptions for broadband, phone lines and, at most of them, mobile service, plus business connectivity and wholesale access sold to rivals. GICS places incumbent carriers here and treats pure mobile operators such as T-Mobile US separately, while fiber-only and satellite network owners sit in Alternative Carriers. Cable companies are classified in Media, not here.

products.name: Mobile service
products.what: Monthly plans for phones and connected devices. For Verizon and AT&T this is the largest revenue line, and postpaid (billed monthly) customers are valued most.
products.examples: Verizon and AT&T mobility, Deutsche Telekom Germany, Telefonica Spain and Brazil

products.name: Fiber broadband
products.what: Home internet over fiber-optic lines to the premises, the incumbent's main answer to cable. It needs large upfront construction spending but is cheap to run once built.
products.examples: AT&T Fiber, Verizon Fios, BT Openreach, Telekom FTTH

products.name: Fixed wireless access
products.what: Home internet delivered over the mobile network to a router. It reuses existing towers and spectrum, so it adds broadband customers without digging streets.

products.name: Business and enterprise networks
products.what: Data connections, cloud networking, security and voice services sold to companies and governments, often under multi-year contracts.
products.examples: Verizon Business, Lumen enterprise networking, BT Business

products.name: Wholesale network access
products.what: Selling use of the carrier's fixed network to rival service providers. Regulators often set or shape the price.

products.name: Legacy copper voice and DSL
products.what: Old phone lines and slower broadband over copper. These customers and revenues are shrinking and carriers want to retire the copper to cut costs.
products.examples: Lumen legacy services, Verizon copper network

terms.meaning: Homes and businesses a network could connect. It measures build-out, while customers show how much of it is sold.
The share of passed premises that actually subscribe. High take-up spreads the fixed cost of a fiber build over more customers.
Fiber to the home or premises: fiber all the way to the customer, as opposed to fiber to a street cabinet with copper for the last stretch.
Home broadband sent over 4G or 5G airwaves instead of a wire. It competes with fiber and cable at lower build cost.
Mobile customers on monthly billing with contracts or device plans. They churn less and spend more than prepaid users.
New customers minus lost ones in a period. The headline growth number for subscribers.
Average revenue per user, usually per month. Rising ARPU shows pricing power or a richer mix.
The share of customers leaving in a period. Low churn lowers the cost of replacing customers and supports margins.
Selling mobile and home broadband in one bundle. Bundled customers tend to leave less often.
Switching off old copper lines once customers move to fiber or wireless. It cuts maintenance cost but needs regulatory approval.
Debt minus cash divided by operating cash earnings. Carriers carry a lot of debt, so this ratio sets their room for dividends and buybacks.
Capital spending as a share of revenue. Networks, spectrum and fiber builds keep it high across the cycle.

drivers.name: Pricing and plan mix
drivers.how: Small price rises and customers moving to premium plans lift ARPU. Because costs are largely fixed, extra revenue falls through to margin.

drivers.name: Fiber build and take-up
drivers.how: Spending on passings comes first and revenue follows as customers sign up. Take-up speed decides when returns appear.

drivers.name: Competition from cable and fixed wireless
drivers.how: Rivals compete for the same home and mobile customers, so promotions and churn move subscriber growth and pricing.

drivers.name: Cost cutting and copper retirement
drivers.how: Closing legacy networks and automating service cut operating costs, which can lift EBITDA even when revenue is flat.

drivers.name: Debt and interest costs
drivers.how: High debt makes interest expense and refinancing a large claim on cash flow, so rates and credit ratings shape the dividend and buyback room.

drivers.name: Spectrum and regulation
drivers.how: Airwave purchases are large one-off cash calls, and rules on wholesale prices or mergers can change returns on networks.

business: Revenue comes mainly from monthly mobile and broadband subscriptions, plus enterprise connectivity and wholesale access. At Verizon, the consumer segment produced $106.8bn of 2025 revenue and business $29.1bn [10]. AT&T reports Advanced Connectivity service revenue of $23.9bn in Q3 2026 [2].

Customers are households, companies, public bodies and rival carriers. Verizon's consumer unit had about 116 million wireless retail connections at end-2025, 83% of them postpaid, and about 11 million broadband connections [10]. Enterprise and wholesale customers sign longer contracts and give steadier revenue.

The main costs are network operation and maintenance, labor, spectrum and equipment depreciation, handset subsidies, content in some bundles, and interest on large debts. Verizon's Q3 adjusted EBITDA margin was 40.2% [1], which shows how much revenue is left after operating costs, before the heavy depreciation and interest charges.

Pricing power comes from network quality, bundling and the lack of alternatives where only one or two fixed networks exist. Telefonica reported record-low Spanish churn of 0.7% and ARPU of EUR 90.4 in Spain in Q3, consistent with sticky bundled customers [6]. Fixed wireless and cable limit how far prices can rise [9].

The big assets are fiber and mobile networks, spectrum licenses, buildings and customer relationships; the big liabilities are bonds and leases. Verizon had net unsecured debt of $123.7bn at Q3 [1], AT&T had net debt of $149.8bn [2] and Deutsche Telekom had net debt including leases of EUR 134.2bn [3].

Heavily capital-intensive. AT&T guides 2026 capital investment of $23-24bn [2], Verizon guides $16.0-16.5bn of capex [1] and BT guides GBP 4.2-4.3bn excluding spectrum [7]. Damodaran's US Telecom. Services group spends about 105% of depreciation on capex [11].
overview: We did not find one sourced global revenue total for this sub-industry, so we do not give one. Company scale gives a sense of it: Verizon's Q3 revenue was $34.3bn [1], AT&T's $32.3bn [2] and Deutsche Telekom's EUR 31.1bn [3]. Growth is low: FactSet puts industry revenue growth below 1% in Q3 [4].

The main segments are mobile service, home broadband (fiber, cable-competing copper and fixed wireless), enterprise connectivity and wholesale. In the US, FCC data show 136 million fixed connections at end-2025, of which 53.7% were cable, 29.7% fiber and 9.1% fixed wireless [9]. GICS treats cable as Media, so those cable lines belong to competitors outside this group.

Carriers sit between equipment and spectrum suppliers on one side and households, firms and rival operators on the other. They buy network gear, towers and airwaves, then sell connectivity at retail and wholesale. Regulation often sets terms for wholesale access, as with BT Openreach [7].

The industry has shifted from copper voice lines to mobile and now to fiber. Fiber reached 47% of OECD fixed broadband subscriptions at end-2024, up from 28% in 2019 [12]. AT&T bought Lumen's consumer fiber business in February 2026 [2] and Verizon closed its Frontier purchase, giving it close to 30 million fiber passings [13].

Sales concentrate where incumbents are large: the US, Germany, the UK, Spain and Brazil in this brief. Deutsche Telekom's T-Mobile US unit had Q3 revenue of $23.6bn [3] and Telefonica's Brazil unit had Q3 revenue of EUR 2,712m [6]. We did not find a sourced geographic split for the whole sub-industry.
competition: A handful of national carriers dominate each market, not a large number. The US has AT&T, Verizon and cable companies as the main fixed rivals [9], and the European markets in this brief have BT, Deutsche Telekom and Telefonica as incumbents [7][3][6]. We did not find a sourced global count of competitors.

Verizon is one of the largest US carriers: it reported about 147 million wireless retail connections at end-2025 including FWA (116 million consumer plus 31 million business) [10]. We did not find sourced market-share percentages for the group, so we give none.

Concentrated in the largest players at national level, fragmented below them. Fiber is being built by incumbents and new entrants alike; Verizon's Frontier deal and AT&T's Lumen purchase show consolidation among fixed networks [13][2].

Entry barriers are very high: spectrum licenses, rights of way and tens of billions of dollars of build cost. AT&T plans 2026 capital investment of $23-24bn and over 40 million fiber locations by end-2026 [2], which no small entrant can match nationally.

Economies of scale are large because network, billing and marketing costs are mostly fixed. Verizon's adjusted EBITDA margin reached 40.2% in Q3 [1], and scale also helps in buying spectrum, handsets and equipment.

Mobile and basic broadband are close to commodities, so carriers differentiate by network quality, bundles and service. Verizon's roughly 5.7 million FWA connections and Telefonica's convergent plans show bundling used to differentiate [10][6]. Where fiber is available it tends to beat cable on speed.

Customers have limited power individually but switching is easy in mobile, which is why churn and promotions matter. Suppliers such as equipment makers and spectrum holders have moderate power. Regulators and wholesale buyers also have leverage over price in markets such as the UK [7].
drivers: Revenue growth comes from subscriber gains, price increases, plan mix and new products such as fiber and fixed wireless. Verizon added 314,000 broadband customers in Q3, 155,000 fiber and 159,000 FWA [1], while AT&T added 769,000 internet customers [2]. Total revenue is growing slowly: Verizon +1.5% [1].

Margins depend on network efficiency, customer mix and cost programs. Verizon's EBITDA margin was 40.2% in Q3 [1]. Lumen's adjusted EBITDA excluding special items margin was 26.3% as legacy revenue fell [5]. Higher fiber take-up and copper retirement help margins over time.

Key costs are labor, network maintenance, energy, spectrum amortization, equipment and device subsidies. Lumen says it is accelerating copper decommissioning in Florida, Iowa, Nevada and Utah to cut legacy costs [5]. We did not find a sourced energy cost share for the group.

Highly sensitive to interest rates because debt is large. Damodaran's US Telecom. Services data show debt to EBITDA of 3.85x and interest coverage of 3.61x [14], and AT&T's net debt to EBITDA was 3.13x [2]. Higher rates raise refinancing cost for all of them.

Subscriptions are essential and recurring, so demand barely moves with GDP and unemployment, though business spending and handset upgrades do. Inflation can be partly passed on through price rises, but we did not find a sourced measure of how much. Commodity prices matter little beyond energy and equipment inflation.

Defensive with slow secular change: revenue growth is below 1% at the industry level [4] and the investment cycle is long. The trend is a shift from copper to fiber and fixed wireless rather than a strong cycle, in our view.
financials: Growth is low and uneven. Verizon's Q3 revenue rose 1.5% but adjusted EPS rose 8.3% [1]; AT&T's revenue rose 5.3% and adjusted EPS 20.4% [2]; Lumen's revenue fell 12% [5]. FactSet shows industry revenue growth below 1% for Q3 2026 [4].

Damodaran's US Telecom. Services group (39 firms, January 2026) has a gross margin of 58.82%, an EBITDA margin of 34.70%, an after-tax operating margin of 19.78% and a net margin of 14.20% [15]. That is a broader US set than the GICS sub-industry.

Damodaran puts return on equity for US Telecom. Services at 19.82% [16]. We did not find a sourced industry return on invested capital, so we give none. Equity returns are lifted by heavy debt, in our view.

Leverage is high. Damodaran shows market debt to capital of 48.82% and debt to EBITDA of 3.85x for US Telecom. Services [14]. Verizon's net unsecured debt to EBITDA was 2.3x [1], AT&T's 3.13x [2] and Telefonica's 2.63x [6].

Free cash flow is large at the big carriers. Verizon generated $7.8bn in Q3 and $18.0bn in nine months [1]; AT&T guides 2026 free cash flow of $18bn or more [2]; Deutsche Telekom guides about EUR 20.1bn [3]. Lumen is the exception, with minus $76M in Q3 excluding special items [5].

Capex is high and permanent. Damodaran's group spends 104.92% of depreciation on capex, with net capex of 0.91% of sales [11]. BT's first-half capex was GBP 2.3bn, down 5% [7]. We did not find a sourced capex-to-sales figure for the whole group.

On Damodaran's data, US Telecom. Services trade at 6.54x EV/EBITDA and 12.22x EV/EBIT on the positive-EBITDA set [8]. Its trailing P/E is 16.79 and its forward P/E 26.50, a gap we cannot explain from the page [17]. IYZ, a US telecom ETF, showed a P/E of 14.83 on 25 Nov 2026 [18].
risks: Regulation shapes returns through wholesale price rules, merger review, spectrum policy and approvals to retire copper. Verizon needed California's approval on 15 January 2026 to close Frontier [13], and BT's Openreach is a regulated wholesale network [7]. In our view, this is the risk most specific to this group.

Technology change cuts both ways. Fixed wireless is growing fast and reached 9.1% of US fixed connections [9]. Satellite providers are a possible rival, though none of our opened sources sizes that threat. We expect AI traffic to raise demand for network capacity, which is our judgment, not a sourced figure.

Demographics matter little: connections grow with households. US connections grew 1.9% in 2025 [9] and BT expects to lose about 800,000 Openreach broadband lines in the year [7]. The slow growth reflects market saturation rather than fewer people.

Customers are moving from voice and copper to fiber, mobile data and streaming-style bundles. Take-up of BT's full fibre reached 41% [7] and 29.7% of US fixed connections were fiber [9]. Legacy lines keep declining, which pressures Lumen's legacy revenue [5].

New entrants include cable companies selling mobile, fixed wireless providers and, in Europe, alternative fibre builders. Telefonica reports that it is reorganizing in Germany to return to growth in 2027 [6], showing incumbents under pressure from rivals.

Geopolitical and supply-chain risk is moderate: carriers depend on equipment makers and tariffs can raise costs. We did not open sources that quantify this for the group, so we give no figure. Currency matters for multinationals: Telefonica's Q3 revenue grew 4.8% at real exchange rates but 2.2% at constant rates [6].

Substitutes include satellite internet, fixed wireless from cable operators and Wi-Fi calling replacing voice minutes. Verizon had about 5.7 million FWA connections at end-2025 [10], showing carriers also adopt substitutes themselves.

opportunities: Fiber take-up should raise margins as build spending fades; BT's take-up of 41% and Telekom's record 190,000 new fiber customers in Q3 show demand [7][3].
Convergence and fixed wireless can grow revenue per household; AT&T's 769,000 Q3 internet net adds were a record [2].
Copper retirement and cost programs can lift EBITDA even with flat revenue, as Verizon's record 40.2% margin shows [1][5].
Enterprise networking demand, which we think AI traffic will add to, supports growth lines; Lumen's strategic revenue rose 10% to $1.28bn [5].
threats: Heavy debt limits flexibility if rates stay high; AT&T's net debt to EBITDA is 3.13x [2] and the US group's debt to EBITDA is 3.85x [14].
Fixed wireless and cable competition may cap prices on fiber; fixed wireless already has 9.1% of US fixed connections [9].
Regulators can change wholesale prices or block deals, and revenue growth remains below 1% at the industry level [4].
horizon.assessment: Over three to five years we expect a steady shift from copper to fiber and fixed wireless, with revenue growing slowly and margins improving where carriers retire legacy networks. The winners are likely those with a strong fiber footprint and manageable debt: Verizon, AT&T and Deutsche Telekom reported rising profit and raised guidance this quarter [1][2][3]. The weak points are leveraged balance sheets and shrinking legacy lines, visible at Lumen [5] and in AT&T's 3.13x leverage [2]. This is our judgment from reported results, not a forecast supplied by the companies.

paragraphs: Telecom is a defensive, subscription business, so it feels the business cycle mainly through enterprise spending, handset upgrades and borrowing costs. The Q3 results fit that pattern: Verizon's revenue rose 1.5% while its adjusted EBITDA rose 8.0% [1], and AT&T's revenue rose 5.3% [2]. Across the whole industry FactSet shows revenue growth below 1%, against 14.6% for the S&P 500 [4].

Debt makes rates matter more than the cycle. AT&T's net debt was $149.8bn, or 3.13x EBITDA [2], and Damodaran's US group shows debt to EBITDA of 3.85x [14]. We did not open central-bank or inflation material, so we give no sourced policy-rate path; our judgment is that lower rates help refinancing but do not change growth.

Currency matters for multinationals. Telefonica's Q3 revenue rose 4.8% at real exchange rates but 2.2% at constant rates [6], and Deutsche Telekom reports T-Mobile US revenue of $23.6bn converted to euros [3]. Carriers earning in euros, pounds and reais are exposed to translation effects when they report in a different currency.

Demand for connectivity is structural, but volumes are saturated in developed markets. US fixed connections were 136 million at end-2025, up about 1.7% in a year, and mobile connections were 427 million, up 1.9% [9]. Growth now comes from upgrading connections: 34.9% of US fixed connections ran at 940 Mbps or more [9].

The mix is changing. Fiber reached 47% of OECD fixed broadband subscriptions at end-2024, up from 28% in 2019, and fixed wireless reached 6% [12]. In the US, fiber was 29.7% of fixed connections and fixed wireless 9.1% [9]. We did not find a sourced global market-size figure for this sub-industry.

Cyclicality is low, as customers rarely cancel broadband. The pressure comes from legacy lines: BT expects to lose about 800,000 Openreach broadband lines in the year [7], and Lumen's legacy revenue is shrinking [5]. Demographics barely help, since growth follows household formation. In our view, the long-term prospect is flat connections with a rising share on fiber.

Rivalry is intense but between few players. Verizon had about 147 million wireless retail connections at end-2025 including FWA [10], and AT&T and Verizon each sell mobile, fiber and fixed wireless [1][2]. Threat of new entrants is low: spectrum, rights of way and build cost are high, with AT&T planning $23-24bn of capital investment in 2026 [2].

Buyer power is moderate: individual customers have little leverage but switching is easy, so churn is the gauge. Telefonica's Spanish churn of 0.7% is a record low [6]. Supplier power sits with equipment and spectrum owners, and with regulators in wholesale markets such as BT's Openreach [7].

The threat of substitutes comes from fixed wireless, cable and satellite. Fixed wireless was 9.1% of US fixed connections [9], and cable still held 53.7% [9]. Moats come from scale and bundling: consolidation continues, with AT&T acquiring Lumen's consumer fiber [2] and Verizon closing Frontier for almost 30 million fiber passings [13]. We did not find sourced market shares for the group.

Regulation is the main political factor. Verizon needed all required regulatory approvals, the last from California on 15 January 2026, to close Frontier [13]. BT's Openreach operates as a wholesale network under regulatory oversight and its full fibre target slipped from December 2026 to March 2027 because the company prioritised connecting customers [7].

Technology is reshaping the asset base. Lumen is accelerating copper decommissioning in four states to lower legacy costs [5], and carriers are spending on fiber and fixed wireless. In our view AI traffic is a demand opportunity, though our sources do not size it. Lumen's strategic revenue rose about 10% to $1.28bn [5].

Economic and social factors include the digital divide and the cost of rural coverage. Telefonica reports 5G coverage of 96% in Spain, 99% in Germany, 73% in Brazil and 88% in the UK [6]. We did not open sources on environmental rules, legal liability or cybersecurity, so we do not size those risks. Competition from satellite providers is possible, and we cannot quantify it from our sources.

Margins are high because networks are costly to build but cheap to run. Damodaran's US Telecom. Services data (January 2026) show a gross margin of 58.82%, an EBITDA margin of 34.70% and a net margin of 14.20% [15]. Verizon's Q3 adjusted EBITDA margin was 40.2% [1], while Lumen's was 26.3% excluding special items [5].

Capital intensity is the offset. Damodaran's group spends 104.92% of depreciation on capex [11], AT&T guides capital investment of $23-24bn in 2026 [2] and Verizon guides $16.0-16.5bn [1]. After that spending, free cash flow is still large at Verizon, with $18.0bn in nine months [1].

Operating leverage is strong because costs are mostly fixed: Verizon's adjusted EBITDA rose 8.0% on 1.5% revenue growth [1]. Returns are helped by debt: Damodaran reports ROE of 19.82% [16] with debt to EBITDA of 3.85x [14]. We did not find a sourced industry ROIC.

Q3 2026 was a good quarter for the large carriers. Verizon raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.04-5.06, its third raise in a row [1]. AT&T's adjusted EPS rose 20.4% to $0.65 and it guides about $2.40 for 2026 [2]. Deutsche Telekom raised adjusted EBITDA AL guidance to about EUR 47.6bn [3].

Telefonica upgraded EBITDA, operating cash flow and free cash flow targets but lowered revenue growth to 1-1.5% [6], and BT reconfirmed adjusted EBITDA of GBP 8.1-8.2bn for FY27 [7]. Lumen reaffirmed 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $3.1-3.3bn but expects business revenue growth only in 2028 [5].

We found no sourced consensus earnings growth for Diversified Telecommunication Services. FactSet's sector figures are dominated by Alphabet and Meta, which pulled Communication Services Q3 growth to 18.3% from 51.5% [4], so they say little about carriers. Our read is that earnings growth here comes from cost cuts and buybacks more than revenue, and that guidance raises are the best evidence of estimate direction.

We did not find a sourced forward P/E for the GICS sub-industry or for the Communication Services sector, and the FactSet text we read gives only the highest and lowest sector multiples. For context, FactSet puts the S&P 500 forward P/E at 17.1 against a 10-year average of 19.1 [4].

The best sourced valuation data are Damodaran's US Telecom. Services figures from January 2026: EV/EBITDA of 6.54x and EV/EBIT of 12.22x on the positive-EBITDA set [8], a trailing P/E of 16.79 and a forward P/E of 26.50 [17]. The gap between trailing and forward is odd and we cannot explain it from the page, so we treat the forward figure with caution.

The iShares U.S. Telecommunications ETF showed a P/E of 14.83 on 25 November 2026 [18], which tracks a Russell index, not GICS. In our read, low EV/EBITDA reflects high debt and heavy capex, and the group looks priced for slow growth. We did not find sourced free cash flow yields, so we give none.

Flow data are thin in our sources. The iShares U.S. Telecommunications ETF held net assets of $445.4M across 21 holdings on 25 November 2026 and charges 0.37% [18]. It tracks a capped Russell 1000 telecommunications index rather than GICS, so it is only a rough proxy for this sub-industry.

Its NAV total return was 10.18% year to date as of 24 November 2026 [18]. We did not open sources on short interest, institutional positioning or breadth, and we did not find the fund's holdings weights, so we make no claim about them.

Capital returns are a visible form of positioning by the companies themselves. AT&T bought back $2.8bn of stock in Q3 and plans about $10bn in 2026 [2]. Deutsche Telekom proposed a EUR 1.10 dividend, up 10%, and up to EUR 2bn of buybacks in 2027 [3], and Telefonica confirmed EUR 0.15 per share [6]. These payouts depend on leverage staying in range.
